A <Term id="vision-language-action-model">vision-language-action (VLA)</Term> model is a robot policy built by adapting a vision-language model to output robot actions. The modules so far covered policies trained from scratch on robot data alone: [behavior cloning](/manipulation/bc-foundations), [ACT](/manipulation/action-chunking), and [Diffusion Policy](/manipulation/diffusion-policy). The VLA line changes the starting point. Instead of training a policy from nothing, take a model that already understands images and language from web-scale pretraining, and teach it to emit robot actions. The design question that defines this lineage is how to get actions out of a model whose output space is text.

The interactive below is an illustrative seven-coordinate action sequence; it is neither a recorded rollout nor a literal tokenizer vocabulary. It places values in 256 uniform bins on a fixed normalized interval and uses synthetic token labels. Drag “Moment in the movement” to see each motion’s nudge land in one of the 256 slots and become a word; the motion buttons and the full 256-slot strip are under “Adjust more”, and the reconstruction error is under “How this was made”. Quantization discards within-bin detail, but error can be zero when a value equals its reconstructed bin center. OpenVLA’s actual bin bounds use training-data quantiles; the toy does not estimate those statistics. <Cite id="openvla-2024" /> Move to another moment and the assigned slot and reconstruction error both track it.
edits.after: A <Term id="vision-language-action-model">vision-language-action (VLA)</Term> model is a robot policy built by adapting a vision-language model to output robot actions. Earlier [behavior cloning](/manipulation/bc-foundations/) and [Diffusion Policy](/manipulation/diffusion-policy/) learned from robot data alone. It starts from a model pretrained on web-scale images and text, and the design question is how to get actions out of a model that outputs text <Cite id="rt2-2023" />.

edits.before: RT-1 (2022) combines an ImageNet-pretrained EfficientNet with a pretrained instruction embedding and FiLM language conditioning. It tokenizes six images: TokenLearner reduces 81 visual tokens per image to eight, yielding 48 tokens for an eight-layer decoder-only transformer with 19M parameters. The paper reports 35M parameters for the full system. <Cite id="rt1-2022" />
edits.after: RT-1 (2022) combines an ImageNet-pretrained EfficientNet <Cite id="efficientnet-2019" />, a pretrained instruction embedding and FiLM language conditioning <Cite id="film-2018" />. Each variable is discretized into 256 bins uniformly spaced within its bounds; training uses categorical cross-entropy over action tokens. <Cite id="rt1-2022" />

Its authors argue that generalization requires both scale and breadth, with sufficiently connected tasks to learn reusable patterns. That is their dataset argument; pooling arbitrary demonstrations carries no guarantee of improving every task. <Cite id="rt1-2022" />

edits.before: RT-1 reports a 3 Hz robot-control rate and predicts the next action instead of an action chunk. Its implementation uses a fixed wait after capturing the state to keep action timing consistent; the paper's implementation details give 280 ms as the maximum observed latency of all components. These are settings of the reported system and set no universal limit on tokenized policies. Its visual and language encoders are pretrained, so describing the whole system as trained on robot data alone would also be misleading. <Cite id="rt1-2022" />
edits.after: RT-1 commands actions at 3 Hz and predicts the next action, with no chunk. A fixed wait of 280 ms, the maximum observed latency of all components, keeps action timing consistent <Cite id="rt1-2022" />.

edits.before: RT-2 (2023) attacked the knowledge problem directly <Cite id="rt2-2023" />. It skips bolting a robot head onto a <Term id="vision-language-model">vision-language model</Term>: each action dimension is discretized into 256 bins, and the bin indices are serialized into the VLM's existing token stream as strings. The two backbones handle the vocabulary differently, which is a detail worth keeping: PaLI-X already has a token for every integer up to 1000, so bins map onto existing number tokens, while PaLM-E overwrites the 256 least frequently used tokens with the action vocabulary. The backbone (PaLI-X or PaLM-E, up to 55B parameters) is then co-fine-tuned on a mixture of robot trajectories and the original web vision-language data. The authors report that mixing the original web data with robot data during co-fine-tuning produces more generalizable policies than fine-tuning on robot data alone <Cite id="rt2-2023" />.
edits.after: RT-2 (2023) brings web knowledge into control <Cite id="rt2-2023" />. Each action dimension is discretized into 256 bins, and the bin indices are serialized as strings into a <Term id="vision-language-model">vision-language model</Term>'s token stream. PaLI-X already has a token for every integer up to 1000, so bins map onto number tokens, while PaLM-E overwrites its 256 least frequently used tokens. The backbone, up to 55B parameters, is co-fine-tuned on robot trajectories and the original web vision-language data, which the authors report generalizes better than robot data alone <Cite id="rt2-2023" />. PaLM-E had already shown positive transfer from joint web-scale language, vision and visual-language training <Cite id="palm-e-2023" />.

Plan: pick rxbar chocolate.” The abstract also gives choosing a rock as an improvised hammer as a multi-stage semantic-reasoning example. This is more specific than claiming that ordinary action decoding automatically supplies a reasoning trace. <Cite id="rt2-2023" />

## Where this leaves the field

These studies demonstrate particular transfers from web pretraining and pooled robot data; universal improvement from scale alone is a stronger claim than they support. Their action interfaces, data mixtures, input modalities and execution protocols differ. Read the reported token-generation rates and robot-control rates separately, and compare results only with their task and evaluation settings attached. <Cite id="rt2-2023" /> <Cite id="openvla-2024" />

edits.before: Treat “VLA” as two decisions behind one label. The first is the prior: which visual, language and robot experience the backbone brings to the task. A large semantic prior can improve instruction following while a poor action interface still makes the system unusable at contact. OpenVLA-OFT is the clean example because changing the decoding and action head materially changed both throughput and success without replacing the underlying VLA <Cite id="openvla-oft-2025" />.
